Replay a fixed set of recorded inputs, at least 200, against the changed template. Block release if schema checks or output checks regress.
For a single-service prototype with one copy and no shared prompts, a full registry may be overkill. Add it when prompts are shared or production changes need tracing and rollback.

concepts.example: A form letter with a required name field; missing name stops the send.
concepts.plain: A template is a reusable instruction sheet with blanks. The system fills the blanks and checks none are missing before sending it.
concepts.title: Template, not concatenation

concepts.example: classify@3:a1b2c3d4 in the log points to one exact prompt.
concepts.plain: Each template and its blanks get a version label. Logs record that label so you know which instructions produced a result and can replay old ones.
concepts.title: Version the rendered contract

concepts.example: Put a pasted ticket inside <ticket>...</ticket>, not loose in the instructions.
concepts.plain: User text can contain hidden instructions, so put it inside clear labels. Tell the system labelled content is data, and cap its size.
concepts.title: Untrusted values stay data

4.02.intro: This lesson is about keeping AI instructions in named, versioned templates instead of pasting them into code. Beginners should care because this prevents silent breakage and makes changes easy to trace and undo.

answers: Because generation predicts which string shape usually follows the question; with no row to read and no uncertainty flag, a policy number and a day window complete plausibly even though the policy was never in training.

Decoding noise: more context does not change the random sampling that makes the same prompt answer differently above temperature zero, which needs lower-variance decoding instead. Prompt pressure and entity confusion in the question are likewise not fixed by length.

Because token probabilities measure fluency, not truth; a fabricated citation can be generated with higher confidence than a correct one, so grounded systems verify claims against retrieved text rather than trusting self-reported certainty.

Replay questions with the current authoritative source attached and check what was actually returned: if the correct chunk was retrieved and the answer still matches an old figure, that is stale parametric knowledge; if the right chunk never came back, it is a retrieval failure, so track rates per document collection.

It tells you how often the system refuses, which accuracy hides entirely; report abstention beside accuracy and citation validity, and alert on abstention spikes because a sudden rise usually means ingestion lag or an embedding change, not model regression.

Because five samples can agree on the same invented policy number; agreement at temperature 0.7 is a proxy for stability, not proof of correctness, so pair it with checks that cited IDs resolve to real chunks.

concepts.example: Asked about a bereavement refund, the bank assistant cited 'Policy 14.3, 90 days'; no such policy existed. The number and the window were completed from the shape of such answers, not looked up.
concepts.plain: The model guesses word by word which string usually follows your question; there is no table row to read, no source to open, and no built-in I-do-not-know flag. Smooth sentences and a confident tone prove nothing about the facts.
concepts.title: Prediction is not lookup

concepts.example: Replaying 200 logged bank questions found 41% knowledge gaps, 22% citing retired 2023 guidance, and 15% merging two products; that mix chose retrieval, not a new prompt.
concepts.plain: Wrong answers come in five types: a fact never learned, a fact updated after training, similar names blended together, a question steering agreement, or random wobble in how words are picked (temperature above zero). Each has a different fix, so name the type first.
concepts.title: Five failure classes

concepts.example: The bank required every cited clause ID to resolve against a current policy document before showing the answer; fabricated citations fell from 19% to 2%.
concepts.plain: The model's own certainty scores measure how familiar a phrase sounds, not whether it is true, so an invented citation can outscore a correct one. Check claims against the actual text you fetched and keep a visible not-found route.
concepts.title: Confidence is not calibrated

5.01.intro: A text model finishes sentences; it does not fact-check them, so confident nonsense is normal behaviour, not a glitch. This matters because rewording the prompt cannot fix an invented fact; naming the failure type first tells you whether retrieval, verification, or a refusal is the right fix.

answers: RAG solves facts outside training, private documents, recent changes, and the need for a checkable source; it moves the failure from invented facts to badly retrieved ones, and does not fix reasoning limits, entity confusion in the question, or ignored instructions.
Because if the authoritative section is not in the returned passages, no wording can make the model cite it; the procedure measures recall at five passages first, then tunes the prompt.
Generation still does what it always does: it produces a confident answer from the weak context, so a threshold that lets garbage through keeps the hallucination behind a veneer of evidence.

It turns invented references into caught-and-refused ones: every cited ID is checked against the passages actually retrieved, and if none validate, the system returns the not-found answer instead of publishing a plausible fake.
When the task needs arithmetic over many records or rigid policy logic; retrieval supplies evidence, not judgement, so a SQL query or fixed workflow is cheaper and exactly correct.

A low-confidence guess from an empty or weak context invites invention, while an honest not-found tells the user the evidence is missing, keeps citations verifiable, and signals index problems; the threshold is applied before generation for exactly this reason.

concepts.example: A nurse asks about a drug's maximum dose; retrieval returns four of the hospital's 1,900 sections as [1]-[4], and the answer must cite one of those numbers or abstain.
concepts.plain: First, turn the question into numbers that encode its wording (an embedding) and fetch the closest stored paragraphs, each tagged with an ID. Then the model answers only from those numbered passages. The library is built offline, so live questions stay fast.
concepts.title: Retrieve, then generate

concepts.example: Asking for average invoice totals over 10,000 rows: one SQL AVG() answers exactly; retrieved invoice PDFs supply numbers the model then fumbles to add.
concepts.plain: Retrieval cures missing, private, or recent facts and gives a source to verify. It cannot cure weak reasoning, a confused question, or ignored instructions: counting rows is a database job, and a fixed house style is a fine-tuning job.
concepts.title: What RAG actually fixes

concepts.example: In the hospital set, 9% of answers cited a section that was never retrieved; abstaining below 0.72 similarity turned those invented references into visible not-found responses.
concepts.plain: A poor index loses the right paragraph, splits it in half, or cannot match your question's vocabulary, and the model then answers confidently from the weak scraps it got. So you need a score cut-off below which the system abstains and separate grading for retrieval.
concepts.title: The cost of a bad index

5.02.intro: Retrieval-augmented generation copies matching paragraphs from your documents into the prompt so the model answers from them instead of guessing from memory. It is the cheapest way to add private or current knowledge and produce evidence a user can check, but it trades invented facts for badly retrieved ones.

answers: Because each model arranges meaning differently; two 1,536-dimension models produce incompatible spaces, so querying index vectors from one model with another embedder yields near-random neighbours.

OCR, summarisation, and parent-document expansion belong offline or in a cache; in the worked example, removing article summarisation from the online path cut p95 latency from 4.8 seconds to 3.1 seconds.
Stored citations point to the wrong or missing passages; stamping chunk IDs with the manifest version lets a citation be traced to the exact build, and old answers stay tied to the old manifest.

Run the frozen regression question set, such as the 300-question suite, before the switch and alert on shifts in retrieval score distributions; a parser that drops table text shows up as a sudden mean-score drop, not an error.

Because an in-place rebuild leaves part of the traffic searching old vectors mid-rebuild; blue-green builds a full candidate, evaluates it on a frozen question set, then flips a routing flag atomically.

The manifest (index) ID that served the request, the retrieved chunk IDs with their top-k similarity scores, which cited IDs resolved, the abstention decision, and the time each stage took, enough to tell a retrieval miss from a generation error.

concepts.example: If new chunks arrive without a source URI field, matches still score normally but every citation links to nothing, and users cannot check the answer's origin.
concepts.plain: The builder fetches, cleans, slices, and stores documents; the answerer turns a question into matches, writes, and checks the reply. They communicate only through an agreed field list for every stored passage, the schema; break it and retrieval fails quietly.
concepts.title: Two pipelines, one contract

concepts.example: The media company rebuilt its index with text-embedding-3-large while the query path moved to text-embedding-3-small; both are 1,536 numbers long, so nothing errored as quality fell.
concepts.plain: The embedder, the model turning text into numbers, must match between building the index and answering queries, and so must chunk size and parser. Record them in an index manifest (a version list), stamp every chunk with it, and rebuild the index on change.
concepts.title: Versions that must agree

concepts.example: Moving article summarisation off the request path cut p95 latency from 4.8 to 3.1 seconds, against stage budgets like 30 ms for vector search and 1,500 ms for generation.
concepts.plain: Give each live step an explicit time limit in milliseconds; writing the answer dominates the budget while search and filters are tiny. Slow work like OCR, teaching software to read scanned pages, or summarising belongs offline, and every online call needs a timeout.
concepts.title: Where the latency goes

5.03.intro: A RAG system is really two machines: one builds the searchable library offline, the other answers questions live. Most incidents hide in how the two are wired together, so recording the exact version of every part tells you which change silently broke an answer.

answers: Because the model learned position from co-occurrence in text, not from a dictionary: 'cancel my subscription' and 'stop the plan renewing' appear in similar situations, so their vectors point the same way even with zero shared words.
Recall at 10 measures whether the correct passage made it into the ten retrieved at all; final-answer accuracy hides that, because a passage the retriever missed can never be cited by the generator.

Because score distributions differ by model, document length, and language, so 0.72 may be a good cut-off for one model and useless for another; thresholds must be calibrated on labelled pairs for your own model and corpus.

Because a chunk longer than the model's input limit, say a 1,100-token clause against a 512-token cap, is silently cut before embedding, so its second half is unsearchable; it looks like bad chunking until you compare chunk token counts to the model maximum, and splitting at section boundaries lifted recall 0.61 to 0.70.

When it measures better on your own queries or the cost fits: the 768-dimension domain-tuned model beat the general large API embedder 0.74 versus 0.61 on the lawyer set, and fewer dimensions means cheaper storage and search.

Because different models, and updated versions, place text in incompatible spaces even at matching dimensions, mixing them gives near-random neighbours; pin the model version in the index manifest and key any cache by version.

concepts.example: The sample code scores 'How long until I get my money back?' against two lines: 'Refunds are paid within five working days' outranks 'A chargeback is a disputed card payment' despite sharing no keywords.
concepts.plain: Each phrase maps to a point in a big space, recorded as a fixed list of numbers (often hundreds of them), and phrases used in similar situations land near each other. Cosine similarity compares the direction two lists point, ignoring their length.
concepts.title: Meaning as geometry

concepts.example: On 150 lawyer-written queries, the general 1,536-dimension API embedder hit recall@10 of 0.61 and a 768-dimension legal model hit 0.74, but the better one needed a GPU and added 90 ms per batch.
concepts.plain: Skip public scoreboards: run two or three candidates over your own 100-300 questions and record how often the right passage lands in the top results (recall), plus speed, length limits, and price. More dimensions (numbers per list) help slightly but cost storage and search.
concepts.title: Choosing a model

concepts.example: The script prints '0.612 Refunds are paid within five working days'; those digits only rank passages for this exact model, so copying 0.72 from another model's docs is guessing.
concepts.plain: A similarity of 0.81 means two number lists point nearly the same way, not an 81% chance of relevance. Cut-offs do not carry across models and drift with text length, so tune yours on labelled question-passage pairs and watch the score spread per collection.
concepts.title: Scores are not probabilities

5.04.intro: Embeddings turn sentences into lists of numbers so that similar meaning means near position, and that geometry is what your search actually sees. Nothing downstream can rescue a passage the retriever never returned, so choosing and testing these models decides what your app can know at all.

answers: Approximation trades some true matches for speed by design, so missing a known answer is expected rather than a defect. You set a recall target and tune M and ef_search until measured recall against exact search clears it inside the latency budget.

It ranks over the whole corpus and then discards non-matching rows, so a tenant holding 1% of the chunks can be left with three results instead of ten. The lesson notes a tenant with 1% of the corpus may return three results rather than ten.

Measured numbers: pgvector still misses the p95 latency or recall target after HNSW tuning, and you need billions of vectors, specialised quantisation, or search that scales independently. Managed services also cost an extra network hop and some operational work.

Raising ef_search makes the search visit more of the graph, so it recovers neighbours it was skipping, but each query does more work. The case study went from 0.62 recall at 40 ms p95 to 0.91 at 85 ms, still inside the 150 ms budget, though 120 ms was its tripwire.

It must prove the data and the index come back usable, not merely that a file exists: restore, confirm filtered search returns expected chunks at your recall target, and record how long a full index rebuild takes. A rebuild measured in hours, such as nine, is an availability risk.

Alert whenever a filtered query returns fewer rows than k and run periodic per-tenant probes with known answers, checking result counts and recall. Do not rely on error rate alone; an under-returning filtered query reports no error and looks successful.

concepts.example: Set hnsw.ef_search = 40 versus 120 on the same table: the lesson's case measured recall 0.62 at 40 ms p95, and 0.91 at 85 ms p95.
concepts.plain: It stores each passage's number-list plus labels like owner or date, and answers which lists look most like the question. Search is approximate, meaning it may skip a few true matches to reply faster. It also applies filters, so some rows are never eligible.
concepts.title: What the database actually does

concepts.example: WHERE tenant_id = '9f2c' AND created_at >= '2026-01-01' ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 10: pgvector applies these predicates while searching.
concepts.plain: A filter is a rule like 'only this customer's rows'. Post-filtering searches everything first and throws away what fails, so a small customer can get three answers instead of ten. Pre-filtering searches only the permitted rows, so results stay correct and usable.
concepts.title: Filtering changes everything

concepts.example: The SaaS case measured 200 QPS at 40 ms p95 and set two tripwires: revisit if p95 crosses 120 ms or the vector count triples.
concepts.plain: One product can be the vector store and the app's ordinary database at once, as pgvector does, so permissions, transactions, and backups stay shared. A separate vector database adds features but also another system to back up and cover on call. Choose from measured numbers.
concepts.title: Choosing a store

5.05.intro: This database is what turns 'find the passages that mean this' into a fast lookup over millions of stored text snippets. It matters because a search that quietly skips the right snippet makes your assistant look wrong even when the model is fine. Tenants, freshness rules, and backup time shape the choice as much as speed.

answers: A path stops identifying the same document the moment it is moved or renamed, creating duplicates and citations that point at an old location. Use the source system's own ID together with the connector name, which survives renames.
Retry the whole batch instead of guessing how far it got, because re-running produces the same index: the hash check skips unchanged documents and ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE replaces the rest.

A 503 is a temporary source failure, not proof that a document was deleted, so deleting index entries on one failed fetch turns an outage into data loss. Retry with bounded backoff and a dead-letter queue; only reconciliation against a successful crawl should tombstone.
Instead of writing every permitted username on every chunk, you store the group IDs and resolve the user's groups at query time, which costs less storage and less re-writing when staff change.

That a large unexpected tombstone count is an incident, not routine cleanup: the source or delta query probably misreported, and hard deletion is held for 30 days precisely so such a run can be caught and reversed.

Enforcement can only test metadata that exists, and retrieval has nothing to check against later. The lesson is explicit: permissions missing at ingestion cannot be reconstructed at query time, so they must be captured per chunk from the source.

concepts.example: sync_document() returns 'unchanged' when hashlib.sha256(body).hexdigest() equals the stored digest, skipping the embedding call.
concepts.plain: Each file needs an ID that survives moves and renames, usually the number the source system already uses. A content hash, a text fingerprint, shows what really changed, so unchanged files are skipped. Rerunning the job then leaves the index as it was.
concepts.title: Stable identity and change detection

concepts.example: Nightly ACL refresh re-syncs group IDs, so a leaver in 'payroll-team-uk' stops seeing chunks marked with that group.
concepts.plain: Every stored passage needs a list of who may see it, because search cannot enforce a rule nobody wrote down. Storing group IDs, such as a payroll-team list, is cheaper than repeating hundreds of individual names. Those lists have to be refreshed when access changes.
concepts.title: Permissions travel with the document

concepts.example: One weekly reconciliation pass tombstoned 1,100 orphaned chunks; vectors are hard-deleted after 30 days, and a run deleting over 2% of the corpus alerts.
concepts.plain: A rename should not create a second copy. Deletions need a separate job that finds passages still indexed although gone from the source. Failures get limited retries and a dead-letter queue, a holding area, so a glitch never wipes real entries.
concepts.title: Deletes, renames, and failures

5.06.intro: Real files get renamed, edited, unshared, and deleted daily, and your search copy has to keep up. This lesson is about the sync job that tracks those changes and carries permissions along. It matters because a stale or leaked copy answers confidently from text nobody can open any more.

answers: A document ID alone points at a whole file, possibly 200 pages, which no user can verify. The page number and section path narrow the citation to the exact paragraph, and citation numbers start at page 1.

Compare extracted characters with the page area: a page yielding only a few dozen characters, under roughly 50 to 100 per 1,000 square points, is probably an image. Confirm by checking whether a page image exists, and by running OCR and seeing whether genuine text appears.

Two-column and footer text coming out in the wrong order, and tables flattened into one unreadable line. A layout-aware parser reads positions and recovers rows, columns, and headings, which OCR cannot fix because it only turns images into characters.

The chunk text is what gets quoted back, so a rewritten or summarised passage no longer matches anything a user can open and confirm. Processing keeps the original wording; condensing happens later, in context construction, where it can be evaluated.

Average extracted characters per page against expectation, and the share of chunks under 40 characters. Both revealed the insurer's problem: 22% of chunks were tiny because they came from scanned pages, and one table had collapsed into a single unreadable line.

Production notes store the parser, OCR engine, and confidence per page so a bad extraction can be traced and reprocessed. With a recorded version you can re-run only the pages that parser mishandled after an upgrade, instead of re-indexing the whole corpus.

concepts.example: claims_manual.pdf page 137 becomes page=137, section_path='Excess > Motor', text='...' instead of one scrambled string where the excess table was.
concepts.plain: A PDF stores where each glyph sits, not which paragraph or table cell it belongs to, so naive extraction jumbles columns and footers. Reading order, the sequence a person follows, must be rebuilt from those positions. The useful output is structure, not just characters.
concepts.title: Parsing is structure recovery

concepts.example: MIN_CHARS_PER_PAGE = 80; a page returning 34 characters is marked route='ocr' and is never indexed as empty text.
concepts.plain: The same file type can hide typed text or a photographed page. Judge each page by how much text extraction returned versus its size. Pages falling short go to OCR, software that reads letters out of a picture.
concepts.title: Route by quality, not extension

concepts.example: Two copies of renewal_terms.pdf share a normalised-text hash, so only the better-permissioned, newest one is indexed.
concepts.plain: Cleaning means stripping repeated headers and footers, fixing hyphenated line breaks, and squashing spaces. It must not include summarising or improving the wording, because search and quoting depend on the original phrasing. Near-duplicates are collapsed using a hash of the cleaned text.
concepts.title: Normalise without rewriting

5.07.intro: Before text can be searched it has to be pulled out of PDFs, scans, and tables, and that step fails quietly. A flattened table or a scan with no text layer becomes an empty slot no search can fill. This lesson covers layout-aware parsing, routing scans to OCR, and quarantining weak extractions.

answers: Very small chunks match more questions, so recall@5 rises to 86 percent, but they return fragments missing the condition or the referenced noun. The model cannot interpret them, which is why the team standardised on 320-token chunks that scored 84 percent with answer accuracy of 77 percent.

Tables, code blocks, and numbered clauses, plus heading sections. Splitting them puts rows and their values in different chunks, so no single passage proves the answer: the payments team's fixed windows split rows and exception clauses and held recall@5 at 61 percent.

The embedding then represents the passage together with where it sits, such as the title 'Card scheme rules' and path '3D Secure > exemptions', instead of the bare sentences. That is why identical wording in different sections can be told apart.
A stable chunk ID plus section, page, document version, and access scope, with the original file reference kept. Those let a user open the exact page and check the wording against what was cited.

A boundary change invalidates stored embeddings, because the old vectors describe old text spans, so a measured rebuild is required. Production notes version chunking rules with the index, and without re-running recall@5 you cannot tell a better split from a regression.

When you need precise matching and full context at the same time: index small children that match the question sharply but return the parent section so the model sees the whole clause or table. Growing chunks instead averages several topics into one vector and weakens similarity.

concepts.example: The payments team's fixed 512-token windows scored recall@5 61%; heading-aware 320-token chunks reached 84% on the same 60 questions.
concepts.plain: Short passages match a question sharply but may drop the sentence explaining who it refers to. Long ones average several topics into one embedding, the number-list used for matching, so similarity scores blur. Judge size by recall you measured on labelled questions.
concepts.title: Size sets the precision-context trade-off

concepts.example: Card rules split at '## 3D Secure exemptions' rather than at every 1,200th character, which is how table rows get cut in half.
concepts.plain: Headings, clauses, table rows, and code blocks are natural seams because the author marked a change of meaning there. Parse into sections first, then pack whole sentences or rows up to a limit. That limit is characters, not tokens, the word-pieces a model reads.
concepts.title: Split on structure, not character count

concepts.example: ID payments-rules/v2/0042: v3 chunks are written as new identifiers, so citations and deletions for v2 stay auditable.
concepts.plain: Each chunk gets a stable ID built from document, version, and position, which is what makes a citation checkable. Parent-child retrieval searches small children for accuracy but hands the model the larger surrounding section. Rule changes are written as new IDs rather than edits.
concepts.title: Chunks are citation and version units

5.08.intro: Chunking is how you cut documents into the small passages a search can hand back. Cut a table in half and the right answer becomes unprovable; leave a chunk enormous and its number-list blurs several topics together. Size, boundaries, and stored metadata decide what retrieval can possibly find.

answers: The check only compares vector length, so a renamed model or retrained revision that keeps the same dimensions passes it silently. Production notes say to pin the model revision in the index manifest because hosted endpoints can change behaviour without changing the name.

A query prefix helps when queries and documents are asymmetric, meaning a short question must find a long passage, and the search is tuned for that. Do not apply it to documents, because they would then be placed differently from the queries that are supposed to match them.

Resume from the checkpoint, not from scratch: completed batches are recorded by content hash, so already-embedded chunks are skipped and roughly 32 percent of the remaining work re-runs. Alert when a run's failure rate exceeds 2 percent.

Cosine and dot product agree once every vector has length one, which L2-normalising guarantees. Storing normalised vectors while the index computes raw dot products breaks it, and that quietly rewards longer documents.

The nine hours of run time at 3,000 inputs per minute, backfill into a separate collection, dual-writing for two weeks, recall comparison on 300 labelled queries, p95 latency comparison, and the storage change from moving 1,536 dimensions down to 1,024.

Deployment notes go stale and hosted endpoints can change behaviour without changing the name, so the manifest is the only live record of model, revision, dimension, and normalisation. Reading it at query time makes a mismatch fail fast instead of returning plausible-looking neighbours.

concepts.example: Test on 50 query-passage pairs from your own traffic: a 384-dimension model can beat a bigger one on your domain and halve storage.
concepts.plain: The number-list a model produces is only comparable with lists from that same model. Different models differ in training data, language coverage, and how well they match short queries against long passages. So the query and the documents must be converted with the same recipe.
concepts.title: One model, one vector space

concepts.example: Checkpoints are content hashes, so a crashed 2.4-million-chunk run resumes at its last completed batch instead of restarting.
concepts.plain: Providers accept batches of 16 to 256 inputs and cap tokens per minute, so batch by token budget. Truncation drops the end of an over-long chunk without warning, hence count tokens before sending. L2-normalising rescales vectors to length one, the assumption cosine similarity makes.
concepts.title: Batch, truncate, normalise

concepts.example: model=text-embedding-3, revision=2026-02, dim=1024, normalised=true: the service fails fast if the query model does not match.
concepts.plain: Keep a record of exactly what produced the stored vectors: model identifier, revision, dimension, normalisation, and preprocessing. The query path must read that same record before embedding a question. Otherwise the numbers it compares came from different recipes.
concepts.title: Version the index, not just the code

5.09.intro: The number-lists that let a machine judge two passages as similar must come from one recipe every time. This lesson covers pinning the embedding model, batching the work, checking dimensions, and versioning the whole vector collection. It matters because mixing two recipes makes every similarity score meaningless.

answers: recall@50 measures whether the correct passage entered the funnel at all, and if it never did, no prompt or reranker can cite it. precision@5 can look healthy while recall sits near 60 percent, which is why recall is measured on labelled questions before touching prompts.

The correct chunk is retrievable from the index by an exact wording match or a paraphrase, but absent for the raw query. That shows the embedding of the user's phrasing, not the index, caused the miss, so fix it at the rewrite stage rather than re-chunking.

The score floor is applied after LIMIT, so a narrow k can still starve recall. When score distributions vary across the corpus, one fixed cutoff keeps strong regions and discards weak ones, so calibrate the floor on labelled data and widen candidates before thresholding.

For quality, ranking over the whole corpus and discarding afterwards leaves a small tenant with few or no results, since its chunks never reach the top k. For security, other tenants' rows were still fetched, which can leak document existence; filters belong inside the query.

Reranking first, since at about 180 ms it is the largest line in the budget, then fewer passages, then a lexical-only degraded path. Query embedding at 40 ms and metadata filters at 25 ms are cheap and mandatory, so they are cut last or never.

Check the logged retrieved IDs against the labelled chunk. If it never appears in retrieval, it is a missing-evidence failure; if it was retrieved and the answer still ignored or contradicted it, it is a prompt-following failure, which is why IDs, scores, filters, and per-stage timings are recorded.

concepts.example: The utilities bot: the right policy was absent from the top 5 in 31 of 80 audited complaints; raising k to 50 took recall@50 to 0.94.
concepts.plain: The first stage must not lose the correct passage, so pull a wide candidate set, roughly 40 to 100 items. Narrow later, to five or ten, because every extra passage adds tokens, delay, and a chance the model follows an irrelevant instruction.
concepts.title: Recall first, precision second

concepts.example: 'why was I charged twice?' embeds away from 'duplicate authorisation holds are released within five business days' until rewritten.
concepts.plain: Words users type rarely match words in a policy, and similarity search compares the two directly. So rewrite first: drop filler, expand acronyms, add a paraphrase, or resolve a pronoun from the previous turn, meaning the earlier message. Evaluate rewrites as their own stage.
concepts.title: Queries are not questions

concepts.example: Sample budget: 40 ms query embedding, 60 ms vector search, 25 ms metadata filters, 180 ms reranking, inside a two-second answer target.
concepts.plain: Give every stage a time allowance, and set timeouts below it, so one slow hop cannot stall the answer. Cache the number-list for repeated questions, but never across tenants or permission scopes. Log which passages were chosen and how much each stage cost.
concepts.title: Budget the whole path

5.10.intro: Retrieval is the chain that gathers passages before an answer is written: search broadly, drop what the user may not see, rank what survives. Measuring each stage separately turns a vague complaint into one specific fix. It matters because if the right passage never arrives, no clever wording can recover it.

answers: The top 50 is chosen by similarity over the whole corpus, so a small tenant's chunks rarely place. In the law-firm case recall for small matters fell to 31 percent because their chunks never reached the top 50, while large tenants kept most of their slots.

Only a tiny share of the visited neighbourhood is permitted, so the graph turns sparse and traversal wanders through many rejected nodes. Search returns fewer than k rows, or slows badly, which is why eligible rows must be identified before the walk.

The access, freshness, and type fields: tenant_id, classification, department, language, effective_from, and document_version. Tenant and classification in particular are mandatory query parameters enforced by the database, not values extracted or guessed from text.

Comparison then needs a function or guessing about casing and spacing, which blocks index use and forces a table scan. Correctness breaks too, because 'Superseded', 'superseded', and 'supersede' may not match, so expired policy returns as current; encode state as an enum or a validity range instead.

An allowlist rejects any field name not explicitly permitted, as the code raises unsupported filter: {key}, so a typo becomes a visible 400 instead of an unfiltered query. Escaping only neutralises a value's quotes while leaving unknown fields and injected column names accepted.

The applied filter set, returned IDs and scores, and the model revision or index manifest used, plus per-stage timings. Those let you rerun the identical query against the same tenant, effective-date, and version constraints to see the same passages again.

concepts.example: Build the clause as tenant_id = %(tenant_id)s with the value bound, so a caller cannot omit the predicate or slip text into it.
concepts.plain: Fields like tenant_id, the owning customer, and effective_from, a rule's start date, decide who sees which passages. They must come from a system of record, the authoritative source, not a model's guess. Left out, the filter silently stops protecting.
concepts.title: Metadata is policy, not decoration

concepts.example: Small matters fell to 31% recall when other tenants were discarded in Python after the top-50; recall reached 0.89 once conditions moved into SQL.
concepts.plain: An approximate vector index walks a graph of neighbouring vectors to find matches, which assumes most stored vectors are candidates. Filtering after the walk simply discards rows that were never eligible, so permitted passages never surface. Decide eligibility first and rank only inside it.
concepts.title: Filter before you search

concepts.example: status = 'superseded' works with a B-tree index; lower(status) = 'Superseded ' cannot use it and scans the table.
concepts.plain: An index is a sorted structure the database consults instead of reading every row. Wrapping a filter column in a function stops that lookup, and every extra condition adds planning work. Keep filter columns plain and fixed.
concepts.title: Keep filters indexable

5.11.intro: The small labels attached to each stored passage decide which answers a person is allowed to receive. This lesson turns those labels into rules the database applies before it scores anything. It matters because a missing tenant check leaks another customer's text, and no wording in a prompt reliably prevents it.

answers: When every vector is L2-normalised, meaning each is rescaled to length 1: then cosine and dot product rank identically, and squared Euclidean differs only by a monotonic transform.
Because ef_search only sets how many candidates the search keeps in its working list at query time; it does not change how the graph is built, so recall rises on the identical stored index.

IVFFlat groups vectors into lists learned from training data and probes only a subset at query time; if that training sample is not representative, new vectors land in the wrong list and are never looked at.

The score only says two number-lists are close; relevance depends on the model, chunk length, and query type, and length normalisation, boilerplate, and duplicated documents can all inflate it without adding any answer.

Build the new index offline, run the same fixed 1,000-query benchmark against exact search to compare recall@10 and p95, and only shift traffic over once the smallest setting clears the recall target inside the latency budget.
IVFFlat, because it builds faster and uses less memory than HNSW, which suits frequent rebuilds; the catch is you must retrain its lists on representative current data or recall drops.

concepts.example: Two chunks of one article, one twice as long: dot product ranks the longer first, cosine treats them as equally close.
concepts.plain: There are several ways to measure how close two vectors are: angle, dot product, or straight-line distance. Each rewards something different, so the choice quietly decides your results. Vectors are the number lists that stand in for text.
concepts.title: Metrics encode assumptions

concepts.example: 1.1 million chunks: exact search took 780 ms; ef_search 64 gave 0.91 recall in 18 ms, ef_search 128 gave 0.98 in 34 ms.
concepts.plain: Exact search checks every stored vector, which gets slow at scale. Approximate indexes skip most of them on purpose, trading a few missed neighbours for speed. Tuning means choosing how much to skip until results are good and fast enough.
concepts.title: Approximate means tuned

concepts.example: A boilerplate footer scored 0.86 against every question, beating the real answer at 0.74 - repeated text inflating similarity, not relevance.
concepts.plain: A score of 0.8 is not an 80% chance the passage is correct. Similar text in any collection scores high naturally, so a number only means something beside the other scores from the same query and the same model.
concepts.title: Scores are not probabilities

5.12.intro: Retrieval hands back a list of passages, each with a match score, and this lesson explains what those numbers really mean. Misreading them is how teams pick bad cutoffs and then blame the model for what was actually a search failure.

answers: An embedding smashes a string into a general meaning vector, so a rare code like 'AX-4471-B' carries almost no signal and behaves like noise; BM25 rewards exact term overlap and rarity, so that unique token dominates. Measured on the parts corpus: 0.34 versus 0.92 recall@10 on part numbers.

RRF keeps only each item's rank and throws away score magnitude, so a confident exact match and a weak neighbour contribute the same when their ranks are equal. That loss matters when one retriever's confidence is real information, such as a single exact code hit surrounded by weak paraphrases.

Fusion blends both lists, so leaning on the dense side (0.7 dense, 0.3 lexical) lets many near-miss paraphrases outrank the one exact code hit; blended recall climbs while identifier accuracy falls, which the lesson calls unacceptable for support or compliance.

Because fusing lists built under different scopes lets the unfiltered retriever leak another tenant's titles or text into the merged result, so both must apply identical tenant and permission filters behind one interface with the same candidate limit.

When labelled data shows a specific class that needs lexical dominance and RRF leaves it below target. Weighted fusion can beat RRF, but only after min-max normalisation, and it stays sensitive to outliers and per-query score ranges, so the calibration has to be measured.

A change to the embedding model, the lexical analyser settings (language, stemming, tokenisation), or the corpus language mix and query-class distribution, such as a new document set full of part numbers. Re-benchmark per class and re-record the weights in the index manifest.

concepts.example: For 'AX-4471-B' dense recall@10 is 0.34 and BM25 is 0.92; for 'how do I cancel my plan' the numbers flip to 0.81 and 0.29.
concepts.plain: One search method matches the words you typed; the other matches the idea behind them. Each misses what the other catches, so run them separately on grouped question types first to see which one is actually failing.
concepts.title: Two retrievers, two failure modes

concepts.example: Reciprocal rank fusion at k=60 weights rank 1 as 1/61 and rank 10 as only 1/70, lifting the two classes to 0.88 and 0.89.
concepts.plain: Merging two ranked lists needs an explicit rule, not an average of scores never designed to be compared. A common rule scores each item by its position in each list, which survives any scale but discards how confident each search was.
concepts.title: Fusion needs a rule

concepts.example: Weights of 0.7 dense and 0.3 lexical lifted blended recall but pushed identifier queries under the team's 0.85 per-class gate, so they kept RRF.
concepts.plain: Split your test questions by type - ordinary wording, product codes, abbreviations, multi-step - and score each group on its own. One blended average can look healthy while a single group quietly gets worse than before.
concepts.title: Tune per query class

5.13.intro: One search method matches the exact words you typed, another matches the idea behind them, and each one reliably fails on different questions. Beginners care because real users ask both kinds, so a single method silently loses a predictable slice of them.

answers: Because it matches the query against vectors computed independently of it, so no passage text is read at query time; that lets it rank thousands of chunks cheaply but only approximately. Its job is to get the answer into the top 50, not to place it first.

It runs question and passage through one transformer with attention spanning both, which only exists once the pair is known, so document vectors cannot be cached. The cost is one inference per candidate, so 50 candidates mean 50 inferences for that query, batched at 16.

A reranker can only reorder the candidates it was handed; a passage the first stage never returned simply is not in the list to rescore. That is why first-stage recall@50 must be measured before tuning any reranker threshold.

Sweep 20, 50, and 100 on the labelled set and plot nDCG@10 against p95 latency and cost, then take the smallest depth that clears the per-class target. The lesson's own sweep showed depth 100 buying only +0.01 nDCG for another 140 ms, which they rejected.

It falls back to the first-stage ordering and still answers rather than failing the request; the code returns candidates[:top_k] on TimeoutError at 0.22 s. That degraded path must be logged and counted in metrics so it is not invisible.

Any embedding model change, reranker model or version change, chunking change, or index and fusion change. Rerun the nDCG@10, p95 latency, and cost-per-thousand benchmark on the fixed labelled set and gate deployment on per-class targets.

concepts.example: Legal corpus: recall@50 was 0.94 but nDCG@10 only 0.61. Reranking the top 40 lifted nDCG@10 to 0.78 - same passages, better order.
concepts.plain: The first search stage compares number-lists computed in advance, which is fast but rough: it finds the right passage yet often parks it near position 17. A slower second pass re-reads that shortlist and repairs the ordering.
concepts.title: Recall, then precision

concepts.example: 40 candidates scored in batches of 16 with 512-token truncation pushed p95 from 180 ms to 268 ms, so depth was capped instead of reranking 500.
concepts.plain: A cross-encoder reads the question and one passage together in a single run and outputs one relevance number. Because nothing can be precomputed for those pairs, 50 candidates means 50 inferences for that one query.
concepts.title: How a cross-encoder scores

concepts.example: Depth 40 gave nDCG@10 of 0.78; depth 100 gave 0.79 for another 140 ms, so they shipped 40 and audit citation accuracy moved from 71% to 84%.
concepts.plain: Rescoring more candidates fixes more orderings, but each extra one adds time and money while the benefit flattens out. So measure the gain on a fixed labelled set and ship the smallest candidate count that clears the target.
concepts.title: Depth, cost, and evidence

5.14.intro: Search returns a shortlist, but only the top few passages ever reach the model, so ordering is a direct quality lever. This lesson adds a slower second pass that re-reads each candidate and shows how to prove it earns the extra latency and cost.

answers: Because the window is shared, so sources packed first can leave no room for the answer; the procedure sets an explicit output reserve (900 tokens in the case study) and gives retrieval only what remains, counted with the model's own tokenizer.

Two near-identical chunks waste budget and make a single fact look better supported than it is, inflating apparent agreement. Deduplication keys on document plus section, and must happen before any per-chunk truncation.

It gets used less reliably, since models attend unevenly across long inputs, which is why the insurer's mid-block eligibility rule produced wrong answers on 9% of reviews. Strongest first and second strongest last, and reshuffling should not move faithfulness more than a point or two.

Keep both sources intact with metadata headers showing which is newer, plus an explicit instruction naming the preferred version. The answer should cite the two contradictory clauses instead of silently merging their text or inventing a synthesis.

A stable source ID, a title, and an effective date (with version) on every source block, so a post-generation check can confirm the cited ID was actually supplied and that the quoted claim appears in that text.

When a small, precisely matched chunk lacks the surrounding text needed to be usable and its parent section restores the decisive paragraph. Then it earns its tokens and you drop the weakest other source, since the expansion must stay inside the same budget.

concepts.example: The naive prompt used 13,400 tokens and repeated one clause three times; reserving 900 for output and keeping six sources cut it to 7,800 and p95 by 600 ms.
concepts.plain: The model's window is a fixed number of tokens, the units text is measured in, shared by instructions, history, sources, and the answer. Decide the answer's allowance first, then pack only what fits, dropping the weakest whole source.
concepts.title: Context is a budget

concepts.example: The eligibility rule sat mid-block in a 13,400-token prompt; after edge ordering plus dedupe, reviewer groundedness rose from 0.79 to 0.91 over 300 cases.
concepts.plain: Models read the start and end of a long input more carefully than the middle, an effect called lost in the middle. Put the strongest passage first and the second strongest last, keeping every source in one unbroken piece rather than interleaved fragments.
concepts.title: Order carries meaning

concepts.example: Two 'Deductible' chunks dated 2023 and 2025 both score above 0.8; the header date lets the model cite the 2025 one instead of averaging the two.
concepts.plain: Archives hold old and new versions of the same rule, so label each source with its date, keep both passages separate, and tell the model which to prefer and to name the disagreement. Blending them into one paragraph hides the conflict.
concepts.title: Conflicts need a policy

5.15.intro: Retrieval produces candidates, not a prompt: someone must choose which passages go in, in what order, and how much room the answer keeps. Most complaints that the model ignored the document actually start at this assembly step.

answers: Because it only names a source of information without forbidding others, and sets nothing testable: no citation format, no refusal phrase, no rule about instructions inside documents. The bank's prompt 'use the context below to answer' still produced 12% unsupported answers, mostly from general knowledge.

Only supplied sources may support factual claims; every claim carries a bracketed source ID; unsupported questions return a fixed refusal token; text instructions inside sources are treated as data. Drop the refusal clause and you cannot tell missing evidence from a bad answer; drop the injection clause and a retrieved document can redirect the assistant.

The final instruction is followed more reliably than one buried at the top of a long input, so repeating the rules after the sources puts them at the end. It costs extra tokens but measurably improves compliance on deep inputs.

Reject or repair it before a user sees it, and log the event with the trace ID for prompt debugging. The validator must also accept a citation-free INSUFFICIENT_CONTEXT as a valid terminal outcome instead of flagging it as missing citations.

It points to evidence going missing upstream, usually a metadata filter excluding the right document or an index problem, not wording that is too strict. Refusal on payroll questions rose from 2% to 7% and a filtered document was the cause, so they fixed the filter rather than loosening the prompt.

Counting citations rewards any marker, even a wrong or decorative one, so a model can look well-sourced while inventing support. Citation precision measures the share of markers that actually support their sentence, and it is reported alongside refusal rate on unanswerable questions.

concepts.example: The bank added the exact string INSUFFICIENT_CONTEXT plus a ban on estimated figures, and unsupported answers fell from 12% to 3.4% on a 200-question audit.
concepts.plain: The instructions must say four things: use only the supplied passages, attach a source label to every factual sentence, reply with one fixed phrase when the evidence is missing, and treat commands inside a document as text. Each is something code can test.
concepts.title: Four clauses of a grounding contract

concepts.example: The builder appends 'Cite as [S#].' immediately after </sources>, and one cited answer plus one refusal example beat a page of written rules.
concepts.plain: Put lasting rules in the system message, the question in the user message, and the passages inside a clearly delimited block tagged S1, S2, matching the label format your checker parses. Restate the rules after the passages, since the final instruction is followed most reliably.
concepts.title: Structure and placement

concepts.example: valid_citations() returns False for an answer containing [S9] when only six sources were supplied, so that reply is rejected or repaired before any user sees it.
concepts.plain: Asking for references is not the same as verifying them. Software must read each label back, confirm that source exists in what was sent, and check that it supports the sentence, then score the share of citations that genuinely do.
concepts.title: Citations you can check

5.16.intro: Perfect evidence can still produce an invented answer when the prompt leaves room for the model's own prior knowledge. This lesson turns the prompt into a written contract with citations and a refusal phrase, so code can check the output instead of admiring it.

answers: Because a retrieval regression and a prompting improvement cancel out in the blend, so nobody knows which stage to fix. Separate scorecards give recall@10, MRR, and nDCG for retrieval and faithfulness, relevance, and citation precision for generation, each with its own threshold and owner.

That the generator is sound when it receives the right evidence, so the fault is upstream in retrieval or context construction. Injecting gold chunks lifted faithfulness from 0.72 to 0.93, which pointed at the builder truncating every chunk to 400 tokens.

An explicit rubric and measured agreement with human labels on the same sample, reported as Cohen's kappa above roughly 0.6 - their judge reached 0.78. Raw agreement is not enough, because a judge can be near chance on imbalanced labels.

Because refusing when no source exists is a behaviour that must be measured, and an all-answerable set never tests it and can reward invention. The lesson calls for 15 to 25% unanswerable (80 of 400 in the worked example), scored against the fixed refusal token.

Measure today's faithfulness on the fixed labelled set, then set the gate at that baseline plus a margin instead of inventing an aspirational target. The team gated at 0.86 after reaching 0.88, and CI now fails any change that drops below it.

New or edited documents, a shift in the language users actually type, and any prompt, model, chunking, or embedding change. The cadence is quarterly re-sampling plus weekly human review of production traces, with newly confirmed failure cases added to the versioned set.

concepts.example: recall@10 0.86 but faithfulness 0.72; the oracle run with the gold chunk injected hit 0.93, exposing the builder's 400-token truncation rather than a weak generator.
concepts.plain: Measure the search step by counting how often the known-correct passages appear, without any model. Measure the writing step separately on support, relevance, and refusal. Then pass the correct passage in directly to see which stage failed.
concepts.title: Two scorecards

concepts.example: They only trusted the gate after the judge scored kappa 0.78 against two human labellers, and every score now logs the judge model and rubric version.
concepts.plain: A model can grade hundreds of answers cheaply, but you must first check it agrees with people. Hand-label 100 answers and compare using a chance-corrected score, Cohen's kappa; below roughly 0.6 the judge is not ready. Swap answer order too, since judges favour position.
concepts.title: Judges need calibration

concepts.example: 400 questions with 80 unanswerable, 20% held out from prompt tuning, gates pinned at recall 0.85 and faithfulness 0.86 so a drop fails CI.
concepts.plain: Build the test set from real logged questions, version it like code, and include questions with no answer on purpose. Set passing marks from your measured baseline plus a margin and block releases below them. Re-sample quarterly as documents and wording drift.
concepts.title: Data, gates, and drift

5.17.intro: A single overall accuracy number tells you something broke but not where. Scoring the search step and the writing step separately turns a vague regression into a decision about the index, the context builder, or the prompt - and lets those numbers block a release.

answers: The hit list and ranks in the trace: if the gold chunk ID never appears it is retrieval or ingestion, while if it appears with a score but sits outside the top few (ranked eighth) it is ranking or context construction. The diagnose helper encodes exactly that as a set test versus a top-3 test.

Because the changed file's new chunks are written while the deleted or renamed document's old chunks stay in the index and remain searchable. This index drift is why document counts and index versions are checked first and reconciled against the source system nightly.

Both versions score highly and land in one context, and when the builder drops the updated_at date the model averages them into a single confident figure. The fix is effective-date filtering, dates in each source header, and an instruction to prefer the newest and name the conflict.

Because the identical refusal appears when a permission or metadata filter hid the right document, so refusal rate alone cannot separate a strict prompt from missing evidence. You check whether the gold chunk was in the retrieved set; the bank's 2% to 7% rise came from an excluded document.

The retrieved candidate IDs with their scores, the filters applied, the index version and embedding model identifiers, and the final order in the assembled prompt, all under one trace ID. Without IDs, scores, and order the diagnosis becomes opinion.

An oracle run injects the gold chunk straight into the generator, so it cannot detect index and ingestion failures where that chunk was never written, parsed badly, or went stale. Next you inspect the ingest side: source versus index document counts, index version, embedding model identifiers, and parser output.

concepts.example: diagnose() returns 'ranking' when the gold ID is in the hits but not in ids[:3], and 'over_refusal' when INSUFFICIENT_CONTEXT appears with the gold chunk present.
concepts.plain: Look first at which passages were fetched, not at the wording of the prompt. If the right one is absent it is a search problem; present at position 8 it is an ordering problem; at the top but unused it is a prompt problem.
concepts.title: Attribute before you fix

concepts.example: Reindexing only the changed file leaves its old chunks live, so nightly reconciliation of source versus index document counts plus ingest-failure alerts is what surfaces the drift.
concepts.plain: Content can be broken before search even runs: a document changed and nothing reindexed, a table mangled by the program that converts files to text, or a chunk holding only a heading. Count stored documents and check version labels first.
concepts.title: Index and ingestion failures

concepts.example: The airline replied GBP 35 from a 2022 chunk while policy said GBP 50; date filtering plus 'prefer newest' took version correctness from 0.81 to 0.94 on 120 questions.
concepts.plain: Even with good passages, too many similar ones thin out attention, contradictory versions get blended into one confident number, and unverified reference labels let invented sources through. Refusing too often is a failure too: it looks safe but stops answering.
concepts.title: Context and generation failures

5.18.intro: A wrong answer went wrong at a specific stage, and each stage leaves a different fingerprint in the trace. Reading those fingerprints is what stops teams from stacking up prompt edits that fix nothing and quietly fight each other.

answers: Because serving reads only a published index alias, so a rebuild in progress stays invisible to users; calling the parser would expose a half-populated index during the six-hour ingest. Writing to refunds_v7 while refunds_v6 stays live means a failed rebuild leaves the old index serving.

Parser version, chunker settings, embedding model, dimension, distance metric, and corpus snapshot. Model and dimension mismatch is caught by the manifest check, which found the query encoder still calling the old model; metric and chunker entries prevent incomparable scores and rankings; the snapshot pins which corpus a benchmark describes and gives rollback a target.

Skipping reranking still returns an answer, just in the rough first-stage order, and the depth sweep showed that ordering was worth only about 0.01 nDCG, making it the cheapest quality to give up. Refusing returns nothing at all, so it sits last in the ladder, used only when no time remains.

The same wording can be legitimate for one tenant and private for another, so question-only keys serve cached replies across tenants and survive permission or index changes. Keys must include index version, tenant, ACL hash, and the normalised question.

One tenant's broken permission filter or stale index, which the global average smooths away - the lesson states plainly that a global average hides one tenant's broken filter. Per-tenant retrieval miss rate, refusal rate, p95 latency, and cost expose it, which is why alerts are set per tenant and query class.

When 5% of live traffic on the new index holds the quality gates without falling below the baseline margin and the manifest check passes, with rollback rehearsed. The canary was decisive there too: it caught nDCG@10 dropping from 0.74 to 0.66 before promotion, and after the encoder fix recall@10 of 0.89 at p95 2.4 s justified the switch.

concepts.example: The rebuild wrote refunds_v7 while refunds_v6 stayed live, and the alias flipped only after the manifest and evaluation passed, so a failed build left the old index serving.
concepts.plain: One pipeline turns files into searchable passages; the other answers questions. The second may only read finished output, never call the converter, and they agree through a manifest recording which model, sizes, and settings produced it.
concepts.title: Two pipelines, one contract

concepts.example: In degrade(), a 2,500 ms budget with 800 ms left returns 'skip_rerank', 500 ms left returns 'cached_answer', and under 200 ms it returns 'refusal' with a retry path.
concepts.plain: Each step of answering gets a slice of one total time allowance: filtering, search, rescoring, packing, writing. If a step runs over, the service drops features in a fixed order instead of failing, and records which path served the request.
concepts.title: Stage budgets and degradation

concepts.example: Keys combine index version, tenant, an ACL hash (a digest of the permission scope), and the normalised question - the check that stopped one tenant's contract text reaching another.
concepts.plain: Every request carries who is asking and what they may see, and that scope must reach filters, caches, and logs. A cache keyed only on question text can hand one customer another's saved answer, so keys also hold tenant, permission, and index-version details.
concepts.title: Isolation, caching, and operations

5.19.intro: A demo breaks the day a six-hour reindex empties the live index or one customer sees another's contract. The fix is unglamorous: versioned artefacts, a time budget per step, and reversible switches, since everything around the model can be made predictable.

answers: A goal with a definition of done, a model that selects the next action, tools that read or change the world, and a runtime that executes actions and feeds observations back.
Because the model can now act: a wrong chat sentence is simply ignored, but a wrong tool call issues a refund or a booking, turning a probabilistic text error into a real change.
Read-only tools are enough when the task only reads public sources; each claim must still pass a citation check, so no write access to the customer database is needed.
The runtime forces it to stop and return partial work with a clear reason, never an invented completion; raise the cap only after traces show more turns are genuinely needed.
Prompts are advice the model can argue with, so a persuasive user message can talk it out of a limit; budgets and permissions enforced in code are guarantees that survive prompt and provider changes.
Run the same ten representative tasks through a chatbot and through the bounded agent, then compare completions, steps per task, cost, latency, and human interventions.

concepts.example: Clinic case: the 78% of questions answered by a policy page went to a chatbot; only the 15% needing a calendar lookup got tools, capped at six steps.
concepts.plain: Four pieces are needed: a clear finish line, a model picking the next move, functions that touch real data, and a runner that executes them and reports back. Remove one and you are left with a chat reply or a single workflow step.
concepts.title: Goal, policy, tools, loop

concepts.example: The sample spec offers suggest, read_only, and confirm_writes, and it refuses refund.create unless confirm_writes is set.
concepts.plain: Autonomy is a range: suggest only, then read data, then write with a human approving, then act alone inside hard limits. More of it means fewer human minutes but less predictable behaviour, so use the smallest amount that works.
concepts.title: Autonomy is a dial, not a switch

concepts.example: Nadia refused unattended booking because one wrong entry costs a patient an hour and a clinician a slot, so confirmation stayed human.
concepts.plain: The runner, not the prompt, enforces the rails: a maximum number of steps, a time limit, a spending cap, tool timeouts, checked arguments, and a log of every observation. Going over budget must return partial work plus a stated reason.
concepts.title: What the runtime must own

6.01.intro: The word agent gets stamped on ordinary chatbots, and the difference decides whether your system can be trusted with real work. This lesson names the four parts that must all be present, then shows how much freedom to grant and who enforces the limits.

answers: Because a multi-turn chatbot is still a chatbot: turns only change the conversation. The test is whether the system can change state that a human would otherwise change.
A wrong credit is worse, because agents fail invisibly: a bad answer is read and ignored, while an issued refund, closed ticket, or sent email must be detected and reversed.
Reads may run unattended since they change nothing, but they still need value-free scope limits: tokens scoped to the acting user and tenant, so one customer's data stays unreachable.
The key is derived from the case and the action, so a repeated request is recognised as the same one and returns the original result instead of performing the write twice.
It needs actor, intent, validated arguments, timestamp, idempotency key, result, and the conversation's trace ID; a chat transcript proves none of that.
Escalation should be cheap and obvious rather than a last resort discovered after an incident, so the human path is a routed option with a named owner from the start.

concepts.example: Reading refund_status changes nothing; calling refund.create moves money, and a wrong one needs a reversal rather than an apology.
concepts.plain: A program that only replies text can be wrong only in its words. A program that writes to live databases can be wrong in the world, so the real test is whether anything changes outside the conversation.
concepts.title: Answer versus action

concepts.example: In the telecom gate the amount limit is tested first, so a GBP 40 credit is refused even before anyone is asked to confirm it.
concepts.plain: An answer sounding certain is not approval to act. A fluent, well-sourced reply can still name the wrong customer, so each action is checked against policy: who may do it, the limit, reversibility, and who approves.
concepts.title: Confidence is not permission

concepts.example: The shadow test produced three duplicate credits after a timeout retry; one idempotency key per case drove duplicates to zero.
concepts.plain: Each action should leave a record like a receipt: who asked, the validated arguments, the timestamp, the result, and the ID of the conversation that caused it. Retries and repetition are normal, so writes must be safe to repeat.
concepts.title: Every action needs a receipt

6.02.intro: Text can be wrong in a harmless way; actions cannot. This lesson separates answering from doing, and shows the approvals, duplicate protection, and records a feature needs the moment it starts changing things on your behalf.

answers: The space of situations is too varied to enumerate in advance, so legitimate runs take different paths; if there is one correct sequence, a workflow is the right choice.

Its stages are fixed, so each branch gets a unit test and the whole route gets a regression suite, with a clear incident boundary; an agent's route varies per run, needing probabilistic trajectory scoring.
The workflow should own the idempotency key and transaction boundary, so it alone commits. If the agent also writes while the workflow retries, you get duplicate side effects.

Agents only pay off where judgement is needed, so a low exception rate keeps expensive paths rare: at 16% the hybrid cut cost to USD 0.021 per invoice, and a drifting exception rate should raise an alert.
It scores the whole sequence of model calls, tool calls, and observations, including tool usefulness, avoided unsafe actions, and stopping in time, none of which a step-level test can see.

When two genuinely open-ended sub-decisions have different tools and risks, such as reconciling conflicting invoices versus finding why a delivery failed: keep the fixed stages in the workflow and give each judgement its own bounded agent.

concepts.example: Invoice parse, validate tax fields, match purchase order, post: with po_match and tax_valid true, route() returns 'workflow' and no model decides anything.
concepts.plain: A workflow runs the same fixed order every time, so identical input takes an identical path. An agent picks each next move from what it just observed, so two runs can differ. Neither is better; they suit different jobs.
concepts.title: Known path versus discovered path

concepts.example: Trajectory scoring asks three things of a run: useful tool choices, no unsafe actions, stopping inside its step budget.
concepts.plain: A fixed pipeline can be tested branch by branch with ordinary unit tests. An agent must be judged on the whole route it took, which costs more and returns a probability rather than a clean pass or fail.
concepts.title: Evaluate what you can reproduce

concepts.example: Only the 16% of 22,000 monthly invoices that failed matching reached the four-step agent, taking cost from USD 0.09 to USD 0.021 each.
concepts.plain: Production systems wrap a small agent inside a fixed pipeline. The pipeline handles sign-in, parsing, validation, routing, retries, and saving; the agent is invoked only for odd cases, with a narrow goal and few tools.
concepts.title: Hybrid is the normal answer

6.03.intro: Not every task needs a model deciding each step, and a fixed pipeline is usually cheaper and easier to test. This lesson tells you when the route is already known, when it must be discovered, and how to combine the two safely.

answers: Because limits written in a prompt are advice a persuasive user message can argue with, and the model cannot reliably count its own steps; runtime enforcement survives prompt edits and provider swaps.
The task, a definition of done a reviewer could test, and the facts the agent must not invent.
A normalised observation uses the fixed error shape the model was taught, so it can tell failure from success and repair its arguments instead of repeating a call that already worked.
Per turn: model, prompt version, token counts, latency, proposed tool, validated arguments, result status, and next decision, grouped by task ID with user, tenant, and policy version.

Appending every message grows without bound, silently raising cost and latency, and only summarising or evicting old observations under a token budget fixes it; the prompt itself cannot cap that growth.
A fixed cut can hide evidence that the call succeeded: the observation truncated at 2,000 characters caused three identical retries and pushed p95 latency to 41 seconds.

concepts.example: The sample AgentState carries task_id, messages, steps, and status, so a missing task_id fails when the object is built, not mid-answer.
concepts.plain: Seven named pieces: the goal, the prompt plus model settings, the callable tools, the runner, saved task facts, safety checks, and the log of decisions. Naming them lets each be tested and replaced on its own.
concepts.title: The seven components

concepts.example: Guardrails sit on both sides: authorisation is checked before settlements.list runs, and the answer is schema-validated before a user sees it.
concepts.plain: Each boundary needs a declared shape for what goes in and out: a proposed call is validated against the tool's schema before it runs, and its result is reshaped for the model to read. Without that, failures leak across as confusing text.
concepts.title: Contracts at every boundary

concepts.example: Grouping spans by task ID is what exposed the fintech agent calling settlements.list with identical arguments three times in a row.
concepts.plain: The step log is a part you design, not leftover debug output. Each turn records the model, prompt version, token counts, latency, proposed tool, validated arguments, result status, and the next decision.
concepts.title: The trace is a first-class component

6.04.intro: An agent is not one clever while loop; it is seven pieces with written agreements between them. Naming each part lets you test one piece, swap one provider, and explain an incident without rereading a long chat transcript.

answers: Completion, deadline, step count, and token spend. Before the model call, because a turn already paid for cannot be refunded and the model cannot be trusted to count its own steps.
A repeat of the same tool name and arguments returns the stored observation instead of running again, so the failing fetch cost four full calls before caching, not one.
Progress means new evidence: a new tool, new arguments, or a new result. Newly worded text is not enough, since the same failing call can be rephrased indefinitely.
It states truthfully that a limit was hit and what was achieved, so the caller can show partial work or escalate; a confident unsupported answer gets acted on and hides which guard fired.
Cost and latency grow every turn because each appended observation is resent, while stale text crowds the context, so the lesson caps sizes and summarises past roughly 60 percent of the window.

Read the spans and stop reason: a bad tool shows repeated identical calls returning the same error or empty result, while a bad prompt shows valid results ignored and blocked outcomes climbing, which is why the lesson alerts on those rates.

concepts.example: The sample loop is range(1, 13): twelve iterations maximum, each appending an observation truncated to 1,200 characters.
concepts.plain: Each pass of the loop asks four things: is the goal met, is budget left, what does the model propose, and is that proposal permitted. The first two are answered before the model is charged for a call.
concepts.title: One iteration, four decisions

concepts.example: Once observations pass roughly 60 percent of the context window, the oldest are summarised or dropped; the research agent capped each one at 1,500 tokens.
concepts.plain: Track whether a turn added anything new: a different tool, different arguments, or a different result. The same call twice earns a cached observation plus a warning, and two turns that add nothing stop the run with partial work.
concepts.title: Progress is measurable

concepts.example: The code returns Result('blocked', 'no new evidence', n) the moment a payload repeats, so nothing further is spent on that task.
concepts.plain: The loop always hands back an object, never a bare sentence: status, answer, evidence, steps used, tokens, cost, and why it stopped. Statuses are completed, budget_exhausted, blocked, or failed, so the caller knows whether to retry.
concepts.title: Exit with a typed result

6.05.intro: The looping step is where agents earn their bad reputation for wandering and overspending. This lesson builds that loop like a scheduler: budget checked first, progress proven each turn, and every ending reported as a stated outcome.

answers: Because the model only emits a structured request and executes nothing. The application validates the arguments, checks the caller's permission and tenant scope, applies a timeout, and then decides whether to run it.
A required field such as merchant_id or a three-letter airport code turns a silent wrong lookup into a visible validation error the model can repair, instead of 50 unfiltered rows being guessed over.

A model may propose several calls in one turn, so each result must carry the provider-assigned call ID; otherwise evidence is matched to the wrong proposal and the next decision is built on a mismatch.

Argument-validation errors, marked retryable with the offending field names, can be fixed by changing arguments; authorisation denials, unknown tools, and outages cannot, and after two failures of a kind the runtime stops.
Never a stack trace, SQL, secrets, or an HTML error page; return only a stable code, a short message, the retryable flag, and which fields were invalid.
Give the write an idempotency key derived from the case and action, so a retry after a timeout is recognised as the same request and returns the original result instead of a second record.

concepts.example: Arguments {'origin': 'LHR', 'destination': 'JFK', 'date': '2026-05-02'} come back as fare_gbp 148.20 under that call's ID.
concepts.plain: One round trip has four messages: the question, the model's proposed tool call with its arguments, the result tagged with the same call ID, and the model's follow-up. The model only proposes; your code decides what runs.
concepts.title: The four-message cycle

concepts.example: search_orders rather than query, an enum for status instead of free text, and a description stating a maximum of 20 results.
concepts.plain: The published name, description, and parameter rules are the only map the model has to what it may call. Precise verbs, required identifiers, and listed choices remove guessing where a loose name leaves it in.
concepts.title: Schemas are prompts with teeth

concepts.example: The code unknown_airport with the three nearest matches let the model fix 'London' to LHR in one turn; failure rate fell from 12 to 1.4 percent.
concepts.plain: A failure should return short, structured feedback the model can act on: a stable code, a brief message, and whether retrying could help. Raw internals teach it nothing and leave it to improvise an answer.
concepts.title: Errors are observations

6.06.intro: A model never runs anything by itself; it writes a request and your program judges it. That one idea drives tool safety, so this lesson covers the message cycle, schemas that prevent guessing, and errors a model can actually recover from.

answers: The description is the only signal the model has when choosing between siblings, so 'Gets data' forces a guess at runtime; even a weaker model picks correctly when each contract says what it returns, what it costs, and what it refuses.

When the narrow ones mirror backend endpoints and make the model chain list_orders, filter_orders and get_order while inventing identifiers: one task-shaped search_orders(query, status, limit) finishes the job in a single call, and tools get split again only when a measured task fails without it.
